I'm working on a game with many 3D UI elements, and I'm trying to create a more modular system to streamline the process. I've encountered several challenges along the way, but my goal is to develop something similar to Unreal Engine's 3D UI system. Ideally, I want a single node that allows you to select the UI and automatically generates all the necessary components, making the workflow much simpler and more efficient. I believe this kind of system should be a default feature in Godot, rather than something we have to build ourselves. It would significantly streamline 3D UI development if we had a built-in tool that, with just one node, could automatically generate all the necessary UI components, similar to how it's done in Unreal Engine. It would make the process much more user-friendly and efficient, especially for complex projects involving lots of 3D UIs.

Here's my own proposal for this feature, which I wrote before realising there was on already.

### Describe the project you are working on

Project Heartbeat, a rhythm game.

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6c92ec2d-8ba7-4991-b1f9-06b0000d38f3)

### Describe the problem or limitation you are having in your project

I originally envisioned the game to use a 3D UI design and originally used viewports projected onto planes, however this comes with a few issues:

- High power consumption on mobile devices.
- Inability to make use of mipmaps.
- Inability to fully take advantage of SDF fonts.
- Complicated input handling.
- Added blurriness due to the reasons above.
- Inability to read the screen texture below you easily (or at all).

### Describe the feature / enhancement and how it helps to overcome the problem or limitation

The ability to make any canvas item be drawn in 3D space.

### Describe how your proposal will work, with code, pseudo-code, mock-ups, and/or diagrams

Currently, I have it implemented in PH's Godot 4.4 fork, let me explain how it works

# Rendering the UI

- Rendering the interface is simple, each canvas gets its own toggle for a 3D transform, which can then be set.
- This 3D data (or 3D info as I call it) is passed around through the whole drawing pipeline for reasons I will explain later. This includes the base 3D transform, as well as the canvas and screen transforms and the view and projection matrices.
- These are simply fed into the CanvasData element of the canvas drawing shader's uniform buffer.

# Culling canvas items

- Generally canvas items that are off screen are culled, if they aren't culled the engine will attempt to draw them, sometimes drawing 0 fragments because they are clipped.
- This presented a problem, since the clipping rects used are all in 2D.
- The solution was to add a second set of clipping rects, these are calculated by taking the four corners of the rect in screen space and making a rect out of them.
- A potential improvement for this would be to add the ability to define a rect for the canvas itself, that way it could cull even more.

# Clipping

In my implementation, only 3D canvases get this special clipping that works in 3D, the rest continue to use the ordinary scissor rect clipping we were already using for 2D.

## Attempt 1: Stencil buffer

- I originally added support to using a stencil buffer.
- This solution was only really going to be viable on hardware that supports dynamically enabling stencil clipping.
- This took a bit to figure out for the backbuffer, but eventually I managed to get it to work flawlessly.
- The problem with this was that you wouldn't always have it available on all platforms, but it worked for the ones I targeted.
- A big pro of the stencil buffer approach is that it's very easy to debug.

## Attempt 2: User clipping planes

- As I understand it's available in Vulkan 1.1 core, so it should be available pretty much everywhere.
- It's in some ways simpler and in some ways harder to implement, unlike OpenGL you don't really have to enable anything Vulkan side, you just add a gl_ClipDistance and fill it (or just set it to something positive) with the values from the plane distance function.
-  To implement this, I added a secondary ring buffer (much like the one we already use for instance uniforms) to store the different clipping planes.
- This ring buffer stores an object that I called a "clip plane set" with 4 clip planes each.
- To use it in the canvas shader, I added a new flag to the batch buffer object and an index to point towards what element of the buffer should be used.
- Then one simply runs the plane equations to calculate the distance to the 4 planes.
- Obviously this could be removed entirely on a per-shader basis using shader variants if performance calls for it (generally I found it to have no to minor impact to 2D rendering).

# Input handling

Input event handling had to be modified a bit but not massively, one important feature to add was the ability to reject mouse inputs that didn't intersect with the canvas plane.

# Potential improvements

A lot of these transforms and values could be cached, but godot itself does seem to already be recalculating some of them every frame, in particular the unprojected rects and the clipping planes would be something good to have cached, but for simplicity of my code (and simplicity of keeping it up to date with godot's stable branches) I didn't add such a feature.

# OpenGL

Currently I've only implemented the clipping planes approach on OpenGL, but I do plan to add it to PH's OpenGL renderer before release.

# Rendering in the editor

I found rendering in the editor to be a bit challenging, because iirc the 2D parts are rendered separatedly from the 3D ones, and the camera transform is not accessible from the 2D part of the editor.

### If this enhancement will not be used often, can it be worked around with a few lines of script?

No, it needs core parts of the engine to be modified.

### Is there a reason why this should be core and not an add-on in the asset library?

It's not possible to implement as an add-on.

I would like to further advocate for @EIREXE's general approach to implementing this feature since I've recently examined their code and how its implemented in a commercial release. It has full transformed UI selection which should satisfy most people wishing to add some stylish pseudo-3D to an otherwise flat user interface. As they pointed out, they also have multiple potential approaches for handling the problem of clipping 2D user interface elements in 3D.

However, speaking as someone very invested into the XR side of Godot, I would like to go a bit further with such an implementation as a mainlined engine feature, since the memory overheads and generally difficult of implementing user interface in XR has particularly been a long-standing pain point. This is something that natively supported 3D UI would significantly improve. For instance, I think it would make a lot of sense to have both both camera-relative and world-relative modes, similar to how Unity implements this feature feature. Furthermore, for people wishing to make fully diagetic user interfaces which are intended to solidly 'exist' in a 3D space, the ability for 3D UIs to respect world occlusion and giving more control over sorting would make a big difference.

Overall I like EIREXE's implementation, and while I think it needs more development before its something which should be formally mainlined, its very solid progress on a long-standing missing feature in Godot.

These are limited to Windows though as they rely on low-level window manager hooks (Lossless Scaling) or driver-level features (AFMF).

You will get the best results by capping the game framerate to a value you can steadily reach, and letting frame generation double the perceived framerate (the `--max-fps` command line argument can be handy). At input framerates of 60 or higher, quality is surprisingly good considering these tools work with the color buffer only (no depth or motion vectors used). Do other languages do this? It sounds pretty novel, hence the possible confusion and pushback. But upon second thought, I do kind of like it?

At the end of the day it's an inline `if`, without the following `else`. It feels like a shorthand. One problem is that, inline `if`s expect a value to be returned and assigned to something _(by default the editor warns about this)_. So this usage goes against the convention.

> or the not recommended
> 
> ```gdscript
> if x: y()
> ```

Just because this way is not recommended doesn't mean you can't use it in your code. Because of the reason I explained above, it's unlikely a "Binary If" will be recommended, too. How do you find `if x: y()` to be less readable?

at first glance
```GDScript
if x: y()
```
looks similar to a variable assignment with static typing:
```GDScript
var x: int = 0
```
. so

```GDScript
y() if x
```
is more readable because it has a distinct if-statement shape

I agree that in expression context, the incomplete ternary operator is quite confusing. While this makes some sense inside assignments:

```gdscript
var a = 1 if b # else a = null
```

in subexpressions it does not make sense:

```gdscript
var a = (1 if b) + 2
```

Note that [null-coalescing operator](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/1321) does not have this problem, since it has a value for both branches.

Admittedly, and I just checked, I presumed that this behavior could've replicated by putting `pass` in the `else` condition:

```GDScript
func _ready():
    free() if true else pass
```

But it turns out this is not possible. You need to explicitly pass a blank statement that does nothing.

```GDScript
func _ready():
    free() if true else "Standalone string"
```

One could argue this doesn't make sense. Although, for the inline `if`, both have got to return a Variant, and `pass` does not return anything. So, under that logic, it does in fact make sense.

> Do other languages do this?

I don't know about other languages, but it exists in Ruby.

One issue aside from the syntax confusion from a readability perspective I also suspect this makes the parser for GDScript more complex and sensitive to issues, as it has to handle both options, possibly doing lookahead and risking problems with how it should handle errors and how it should assume what's intended, should something like `foo() if x bar()` be treated as "expected `else` after ..." or something else? Either suggestion would be confusing if the user intends the other syntax, for example what if they intended:
```gdscript
foo() if x
bar()
```
But the compiler assumed they meant:
```gdscript
foo() if x else bar()
```
Then the user would be given the wrong suggestion

As far as I can tell the two syntaxes aren't completely mutually exclusive and there would be at least some possible error cases where both syntaxes could be expected and confusion would be caused by the parser giving the wrong suggestion

I'd suggest that *if* this is added it should use the `when` keyword instead which is only used for `match` and therefore simple to parse and assume
Adding syntax without purpose to appeal to a few people will make the language as a whole harder to understand. Whether you like the syntax or not, you'll have to learn it to understand others' code.

I don't want to bash the intention of proposer, but from me and also coding best practices from professional programmers: _"if you don't handle the else case in a conditional statement, you are bound to create bugs in code/application"_. 

Hence, proceed with caution on this proposal.

> 
> func _ready():
>     free() if true else pass
> 
> But it turns out this is not possible. You need to explicitly pass a blank statement that does nothing.

You can just do `free() if true else null`.

I don't understand why step 3i fails:

> The new Godot editor instance starts:
> 1. `GDExtension::open_library` tries to delete `~libgdext.windows.x86_64.dll` again. It fails, but ignores the error.

At this point, I think the original Godot instance should be fully shutdown, and so even if you can't `FreeLibrary()` the Go-based DLL, the original process having gone away should mean that the DLL is no longer locked, right?

And if that's not the case, I think trying to figure out why that is, and if we can fix it, would be better than the solution proposed here of making more temporary copies of the DLL. (My concern with making more copies is that we'd need to make sure they get cleaned up at some point.)

> At this point, I think the original Godot instance should be fully shutdown, and so even if you can't `FreeLibrary()` the Go-based DLL, the original process having gone away should mean that the DLL is no longer locked, right?

I haven't investigated the Godot editor's reload mechanism, but I assume that it's impossible for the old Godot to completely shut down first, because then who could launch the new editor? I suspect it shuts down (close/dispose/deconstruct/etc.) as much as possible, then launches the new editor, then closes itself. Because the DLL is held open by the old process itself, this precise order matters.

*If* I'm right about that restart mechanism, then reload could be changed to a three part mechanism as a more general workaround for this class of problem (and maybe there are some other bugs in this class of issue that it would help with too?):

1. The old Godot launches a new Godot process that is tasked with restarting the editor after the old Godot process is gone.
1. The new process doesn't load the project (!), waits until the old process is gone, then launches Godot again with the right parameters to load the project.
1. The new Godot process loads the project, and at this point, the "middle" process still exists, but it hasn't tried to load my GDExtension, so this is ok.

> (My concern with making more copies is that we'd need to make sure they get cleaned up at some point.)

FWIW, I addressed this in the issue and it doesn't concern me.

*Currently* Godot fails to clean up the copy when it fails in this way, so at worst, it's only as bad as it used to be. (Well, maybe more than just one file, if something unrelated also happens that triggers this behavior. But I haven't looked deeply into reloads and I'm concerned that limiting it to two files would hamper some other situations, so I'd rather not do something like that unless there's good reason.)

> I haven't looked deeply into reloads

I found this PR--it seems GDExtension reloading without restarting the editor is meant to work:

* https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/80284

This means that changes to the editor restart process wouldn't be enough to address this proposal, because the editor shouldn't have to restart. There needs to be a way to handle having multiple locked copies of the DLLs files active at the same time (like the suggestion).

---

A more direct change to the proposal to address the cleanup concern could be having an extra `~`-prefix file that keeps track of the list of temp copies that have been created, so the next editor launch can delete them.

> I found this PR--it seems GDExtension reloading without restarting the editor is meant to work:
> 
> * [Implement reloading of GDExtensions godot#80284](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/80284)
> 
> This means that changes to the editor restart process wouldn't be enough to address this proposal, because the editor shouldn't have to restart. There needs to be a way to handle having multiple locked copies of the DLLs files active at the same time (like the suggestion).

Unfortunately, making multiple copies won't help in this case. If we can't `FreeLibrary()`/`dlclose()` the GDExtension, then we can't reload it, because there will be conflicting symbols when trying to load the new copy while the old copy is still loaded.

> > At this point, I think the original Godot instance should be fully shutdown, and so even if you can't `FreeLibrary()` the Go-based DLL, the original process having gone away should mean that the DLL is no longer locked, right?
> 
> I haven't investigated the Godot editor's reload mechanism, but I assume that it's impossible for the old Godot to completely shut down first, because then who could launch the new editor? I suspect it shuts down (close/dispose/deconstruct/etc.) as much as possible, then launches the new editor, then closes itself. Because the DLL is held open by the old process itself, this precise order matters.

I did a little research into this. It looks like you're correct with regard to the order, and needing to have an existing process around to start the new process. I'm not that familiar with Windows, so I was imagining we'd have something like Linux's `exec()`-family of functions that can replace the current process, but it looks like that's not possible on Windows.

On the Godot side, it's `OS::create_instance()` that actually launches the new Godot instance. So, we could conceivably have an `OS_Windows::create_instance()` that took the extra steps to "trampoline" the new Godot into existence after the old one has fully exited?

Unfortunate about loading it multiple times not working. That works fine for my use, I was only shooting for full support so the value of the proposal is a bit stronger. 😅

Another approach came to mind that's maybe simpler than a generalized trampoline: a new editor arg `--wait-until-process-terminated <pid>` (or env variable). The old instance passes its own PID to the new one, the arg delays all of the normal editor startup including GDExtension loading, so (I think) the delete works.

> Another approach came to mind that's maybe simpler than a generalized trampoline: a new editor arg `--wait-until-process-terminated <pid>` (or env variable). The old instance passes its own PID to the new one, the arg delays all of the normal editor startup including GDExtension loading, so (I think) the delete works.

That's an interesting idea! Unless we want to implement that for every platform, we'd need to come up with a nice way to isolate it in the Windows platform code somehow. And, unfortunately, I'm not personally adept enough with Windows to come up with an implementation for that.

> The old instance passes its own PID to the new one, the arg delays all of the normal editor startup

I thought about this some more, and I'm concerned about a race that could happen if the OS schedules things a certain way:

1. The old instance starts the new instance, passing it `--wait-until-process-terminated <old pid>`
2. The old instance stops.
3. A new, unrelated process starts and takes over the old PID. (It's free to use again as soon as the old process is gone.)
4. The new instance finally starts running, and checks to see if `<old pid>` is running. It is! But it's the wrong process.
5. Godot waits to start until the unrelated process is gone--which it might never be. Godot appears frozen.

I figure signaling of some kind is needed to avoid the race.

---

A very simple signal would be for the new process to actually be responsible for killing the old process. The arg would be `--kill-previous-editor-pid <pid>`. Godot already has an external-PID `kill` that can be used. (Although it needs to be enhanced to actually wait for the process to end, not just start the kill.)

I implemented this new approach at https://github.com/31/godot/commit/12c46cf052add71880d419e22d86cd3328f265b3. (Not ready for PR, but want to know if the approach is ok in general.)

On my machine with my simple GDExtension, it seems to work. I implemented it in a way that it should do nothing on non-Windows platforms, because it's not necessary there.
I polished it up a bit and submitted it as a PR to `master` at https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/87165.

@31 I don't like the idea of killing the process. It really doesn't solve the problem you describe, that is: a new unrelated process can still start with the same PID, but now we're killing it, which seems like a worse outcome.

What if it waited for the process, but had a reasonable timeout, where it would give up waiting if it took longer than, say, 5 seconds?
(Replied at https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/87165#issuecomment-1894351209.)

The downside of this approach is that it'll make certain shaders work only if your include paths are correctly set in the Project Settings. This makes it harder to transfer shaders across projects and distribute them on the Asset Library or [Godot Shaders](https://godotshaders.com/).

I think this proposal stems from the fact that we don't have a good way to "find and replace" through all files in a project. For me, what I would do here is open my project in VSCode then find and replace the old include file path with the new path. That workflow works really well in Godot. 

IMO what we need is a way to do that within editor so that:
1. Users don't need to close their project
2. Users don't need to have another IDE in order to clean up their project.
